[[tx-2026-0006]] TRAIGA in force as Business and Commerce Code Chapter 552, enforceable only by the Attorney General
The topic is state policy. The decider is Office of the Attorney General of Texas, a state agency. Its status is decided.
The Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act took effect on January 1st, 2026 as Chapter 552 of the Business and Commerce Code. It bans developing or deploying an AI system with intent to unlawfully discriminate, to manipulate behavior, for social scoring or to produce certain illegal content. It also requires government agencies to tell people when they are interacting with an AI system. The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority and the statute creates no private right of action.
This one is statewide.
June 22nd, 2025, signed, HB 149 signed by the Governor. January 1st, 2026, takes effect, Chapter 552 took effect.
Public access is contact_only. Individuals can't sue under this chapter. The route is a complaint to the Attorney General. The same chapter requires that office to create and maintain an online mechanism on its website through which a consumer may submit a complaint.
The chapter was created by HB 149 and took effect January 1st, 2026, quoted as "Added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1174 (H.B. 149 ), Sec. 4, eff. January 1, 2026.". The Attorney General has exclusive enforcement authority and there is no private right of action, quoted as "(a) The attorney general has exclusive authority to enforce this chapter, except to the extent provided by Section  552.106 . (b) This chapter does not provide a basis for, and is not subject to, a private right of action for a violation of this chapter or any other law.". The statute sets tiered civil penalties by violation type, quoted as "(1) for each violation the court determines to be curable or a breach of a statement submitted to the attorney general under Section  552.104 (b)(2), not less than $10,000 and not more than $12,000; (2) for each violation the court determines to be uncurable, not less than $80,000 and not more than $200,000; and (3) for a continued violation, not less than $2,000 and not more than $40,000 for each day the violation continues.". The discrimination ban turns on intent, and disparate impact alone is not enough to show it, quoted as "(b) A person may not develop or deploy an artificial intelligence system with the intent to unlawfully discriminate against a protected class in violation of state or federal law. (c) For purposes of this section, a disparate impact is not sufficient by itself to demonstrate an intent to discriminate.". Government agencies must disclose AI interaction even when it would be obvious, quoted as "(c) A person is required to make the disclosure under Subsection (b) regardless of whether it would be obvious to a reasonable consumer that the consumer is interacting with an artificial intelligence system.". There is a rebuttable presumption that a person used reasonable care, quoted as "(c) There is a rebuttable presumption that a person used reasonable care as required under this chapter.". The chapter requires the Attorney General to run an online complaint mechanism, quoted as "The attorney general shall create and maintain an online mechanism on the attorney general's Internet website through which a consumer may submit a complaint under this chapter to the attorney general.".

[[tx-2026-0007]] Utilities Code limits how the PUCT may direct ERCOT, and bars verbal directives
The topic is power and the grid. The decider is Texas Legislature, a legislature. Its status is decided.
Texas law restricts the channels through which the Public Utility Commission may order ERCOT to act. A verbal directive is prohibited outright. An official action may be directed only by contested case, by rulemaking or by a written order or memorandum adopted on a majority vote. The ERCOT board selection committee picks ERCOT's directors and designates its chair. The governor does not.
No county is named on the record and it is not marked statewide. It sits on the ERCOT grid.
June 8th, 2021, takes effect, SB 2 (87R) added the board selection committee.
Public access is an open meeting. A directive to ERCOT must run through a contested case, a rulemaking or a majority vote taken in a meeting. Each of those routes carries its own way in for the public. PUCT open meetings are listed on the agency calendar feed and are open to the public in Commissioners Hearing Room 7-100.
The commission may not verbally direct ERCOT and may direct official action only three ways, quoted as "(a) The commission may not use a verbal directive to direct an independent organization certified under Section 39.151 to take an official action. The commission may direct the organization to take an official action only through: (1) a contested case; (2) rulemaking; or (3) a memorandum or written order adopted by a majority vote.". The ERCOT board selection committee is three members, one each appointed by the governor, lieutenant governor and speaker, quoted as "(a) The ERCOT board selection committee is composed of: (1) one member appointed by the governor; (2) one member appointed by the lieutenant governor; and (3) one member appointed by the speaker of the house of representatives.". That committee selects ERCOT's governing body and designates its chair and vice chair, quoted as "(d) The committee shall select members eligible under Section 39.151 to serve on the governing body of an independent organization certified under that section for the ERCOT power region and shall designate the chair and vice chair of the governing body from those members.".

[[tx-2026-0008]] Texas Government Code Chapter 2054 carries three conflicting Subchapter S's on AI, with duplicated section numbers
The topic is state policy. The decider is Texas Legislature, a legislature. Its status is open.
Three separate acts of the 89th Legislature each added a Subchapter S to Government Code Chapter 2054, and two of them number their sections identically. Section 2054.702 exists twice with entirely different commands, as do Sections 2054.701 and 2054.703 through 2054.705. The codifier has flagged the conflict in the published code rather than resolved it. Which text governs a state agency's AI duties is unsettled on the face of the statute.
This one is statewide.
September 1st, 2025, takes effect, Both conflicting AI subchapters took effect.
Public access is contact_only. A codification conflict is resolved either by the Legislature in a future non substantive revision bill or by a court. There is no comment window. A reader who cares can raise it with their own legislator or with the Texas Legislative Council, which prepares the revision bills.
The published code carries an editorial note recording three separate Subchapter S enactments, quoted as "Subchapter S, consisting of Secs. 2054.701 to 2054.713, was added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1148 (S.B.  1964 ), Sec. 5. For another Subchapter S, consisting of Secs. 2054.651 to 2054.654, added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 951 (H.B.  5195 ), Sec. 1, see Sec. 2054.651 et seq., post. For another Subchapter S, consisting of Secs. 2054.701 to 2054.705, added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1079 (H.B.  2818 ), Sec. 1, see Sec. 2054.701 et seq., post.". One version of Section 2054.702 concerns generative AI technology, quoted as "Sec. 2054.702. GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGY.". The other version of Section 2054.702 requires a statewide AI code of ethics, quoted as "Sec. 2054.702. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEM CODE OF ETHICS.  (a) The department by rule shall establish an artificial intelligence system code of ethics for use by state agencies and local governments that procure, develop, deploy, or use artificial intelligence systems.". That code of ethics must align with a named federal framework, quoted as "the artificial intelligence system code of ethics must include guidance for the deployment and use of artificial intelligence systems and heightened scrutiny artificial intelligence systems that aligns with the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology.". Local governments as well as state agencies must adopt the code of ethics, quoted as "(c) State agencies and local governments shall adopt the code of ethics developed under this section.".

[[tx-2026-0009]] DIR must run an AI regulatory sandbox letting state agencies test systems outside normal rules
The topic is state policy. The decider is Texas Department of Information Resources, a state agency. Its status is pending.
The Department of Information Resources is required to establish a program letting eligible public entities contract with registered vendors to test AI systems before deployment. That testing is expressly without full compliance with otherwise applicable regulations. Vendors apply, and participants file quarterly reports. The department must report to the Legislature by November 30th of each even numbered year. That makes November 30th, 2026 the first reporting date.
This one is statewide.
September 1st, 2025, takes effect, SB 1964 took effect. November 30th, 2026, statutory deadline, Department report to the Legislature due, per Sec. 2054.706(g).
Public access is contact_only. The application process runs to vendors registered with DIR rather than to the general public. The statute provides no public comment step. The public visibility point is the report the department owes the Legislature by November 30th, 2026. A reader can ask DIR for the vendor application process and for any quarterly reports already filed.
The sandbox is defined as testing without full regulatory compliance, quoted as ""Program" means the program established by this section that is designed to allow temporary testing of an artificial intelligence system in a controlled, limited manner without requiring full compliance with otherwise applicable regulations.". The department must establish and administer the program, quoted as "(b) The department shall establish and administer a program to support eligible entities in contracting with vendors to engage in research, development, training, testing, and other pre-deployment activities related to artificial intelligence systems". Vendor applications must include a public risk assessment and a mitigation plan, quoted as "(2) a risk assessment of the system that addresses potential impacts on the public; and (3) a plan for mitigating any adverse consequences discovered during the system's testing phase.". The department owes the Legislature a report on a fixed recurring date, quoted as "(g) Not later than November 30 of each even-numbered year, the department shall produce an annual report and submit the report to the legislature summarizing:". The sandbox was created by SB 1964, effective September 1st, 2025, quoted as "Added by Acts 2025, 89th Leg., R.S., Ch. 1148 (S.B.  1964 ), Sec. 5, eff. September 1, 2025.".

[[tx-2026-0012]] TRAIGA preempts city and county regulation of artificial intelligence
The topic is state policy. The decider is Texas Legislature, a legislature. Its status is decided.
Chapter 552 of the Business and Commerce Code supersedes and preempts any local ordinance, resolution, rule or regulation about the use of AI systems. Texas cities and counties that might otherwise write their own AI rules are displaced by the state statute. The preemption is written broadly and without a carve out on its face.
This one is statewide.
January 1st, 2026, takes effect, Chapter 552 took effect, including the preemption section.
Public access is closed. The preemption is enacted law and takes no comment. Changing it takes the Legislature or a court. The Legislature next convenes in regular session in 2027. A resident whose city wants to act on AI can raise it with their legislator.
The chapter preempts local regulation of AI use, quoted as "Sec. 552.003. LOCAL PREEMPTION.  This chapter supersedes and preempts any ordinance, resolution, rule, or other regulation adopted by a political subdivision regarding the use of artificial intelligence systems.".

[[tx-2026-0025]] Statute requires state agencies and local governments to post standardized notice of AI systems
The topic is state policy. The decider is Texas Department of Information Resources, a state agency. Its status is pending.
Every state agency and local government that deploys a public facing AI system must post a standardized notice on the related applications, websites and public computer systems. The same duty covers any system that is a controlling factor in a consequential decision. The Department of Information Resources is required to develop the notice form. That form must describe the system, its data sources and its privacy and ethics safeguards.
This one is statewide.
September 1st, 2025, takes effect, SB 1964 took effect.
Public access is contact_only. The notice is meant to appear wherever the system is used. A resident who meets a government AI system should be able to see one. Where no notice appears, the question goes to the agency or local government running the system. Questions about the form itself go to DIR, which was required to develop it.
Agencies and local governments must post a standardized notice for public facing or consequential AI systems, quoted as "(a) Each state agency and local government deploying or using an artificial intelligence system that is public-facing or that is a controlling factor in a consequential decision shall include a standardized notice on all related applications, Internet websites, and public computer systems.". DIR must develop the notice form and the statute fixes its minimum contents, quoted as "(b) The department shall develop a form that agencies must use for the notice required under Subsection (a). The form must include: (1) general information about the system and data sources the system uses; and (2) measures taken to maintain compliance with information privacy laws and ethics standards.".

[[tx-2026-0026]] Temple Planning and Zoning Commission takes up a Unified Development Code amendment that would require a Conditional Use Permit for every future data center
The topic is data centers. The decider is City of Temple Planning and Zoning Commission, a city. Its status is pending.
The Temple Planning and Zoning Commission has three data center items on its August 17th, 2026 agenda. The central one is a set of proposed Unified Development Code amendments. They would require a Conditional Use Permit for any future data center, even in districts where data centers are already allowed. The city says the change would add a public review step and let Temple attach project specific conditions, technical studies and supporting documentation before a project moves forward. A second item is zoning for a subsequent building in Rowan Digital Infrastructure's first phase at Synergy Industrial Park, which the developer calls Lasso. Temple's own data center hub states that domestic water use for Project Temple is contractually capped at 4,000 gallons per day. It also states that projects under this framework would have to use closed-loop cooling.
The counties named are Bell. It sits on the ERCOT grid.
August 17th, 2026, hearing, Planning and Zoning Commission considers the UDC amendments, the Lasso zoning case and the Synergy Industrial Park plat.
Public access is an open meeting. Attend the Planning and Zoning Commission meeting on August 17th, 2026. Since December 11th, 2025 the City of Temple no longer offers a virtual participation option for board and commission meetings. Attendance is in person at City Hall on North Main Street. Agendas and supporting documents are posted on the city's data center hub and its public meetings page, and the City Secretary's office is reachable at 254-298-5700.
The Temple Planning and Zoning Commission will consider several data center items at its August 17th meeting, quoted as "As a part of that development process, the Temple Planning & Zoning Commission will consider several items related to data center development during its August 17 meeting.". The proposed code amendment would require a Conditional Use Permit for future data centers even where they are already a permitted use, quoted as "The proposed amendments would apply to future proposed projects by requiring a Conditional Use Permit (CUP), even in zoning districts where data centers are otherwise permitted.". The zoning item on the same agenda is a later building in Rowan's first phase, which the developer calls Lasso, quoted as "This is for a subsequent building related to Rowan's initial phase in Synergy Industrial Park. You may see this project referred to as Lasso by Rowan.".
